title: Show the wool
hook: sheep don't show the shepherd their fodder, they show wool (Enchiridion 46)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was quickly: say he bathes quickly, not badly, because you saw the speed but not the reason. Your line was say what you saw.

Somewhere tonight, someone who just finished a book on mindfulness is explaining it at dinner, while visibly not being mindful. Plenty of people have been that someone. You've been on this path a long time now, nearly four hundred days, and it would be natural to want to talk about it. Section forty-six of the handbook has a word for that urge, and then it gives a strange picture: a field of sheep.
screen: `EXPLAINING MINDFULNESS AT DINNER.` → `NEARLY FOUR HUNDRED DAYS IN.` → `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Never call yourself a philosopher, Epictetus says, and don't talk much about your principles among people who haven't asked. Do what follows from them. At a dinner, don't explain how one ought to eat. Eat as one ought. Socrates, he says, had so completely given up showing off that people would come to him asking to be introduced to philosophers, and he would take them. He let himself be overlooked, and didn't mind. Here's the test: when someone tells you that you know nothing, and it doesn't sting, you can know you've begun the work. And if talk among people new to all this turns to principles, mostly keep quiet. There's a danger, he says, of throwing up what you haven't digested yet. That's not a polite image. He means it not to be. Then the sheep. Sheep don't bring their grass back up to show the shepherd how much they've eaten. They digest the pasture inside, and what comes out is wool and milk. So don't show people your principles; show them the actions that come from digesting them. Talk is the grass. Practice is the wool. People can't use your grass. They can use your wool: a moment of patience, a gossip skipped, a promise kept without swearing. After nearly four hundred days, a good sign of this path may be something someone else notices in you, without you ever mentioning where it came from.
screen: `DON'T CALL YOURSELF A PHILOSOPHER.` · `SOCRATES LET HIMSELF BE OVERLOOKED.` · `DON'T THROW UP UNDIGESTED GRASS.` · `SHEEP SHOW WOOL AND MILK.` · then, large: `SHOW THE WOOL.`

segments.voice: Look back over this path, the words, the stories, the practices, and find one thing that has actually changed in how you live: not something you could explain, something you do, like a pause before reacting, a smaller portion, a kinder answer. That's your wool. Hold it quietly, without a word about where it came from.
Pasture. What a sheep digests quietly inside, giving back wool and milk, not the grass itself; show practice, not principles. Today's word.
Your line: practice is the wool. Grass is for digesting; wool is for giving. That's day three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism avoid calling themselves Stoics or explaining philosophy uninvited, and try to let it show in how they act instead.

chat.meaning: Sheep don't bring up grass to show what they ate; they give wool and milk. Show the actions, not the principles.

Socrates.meaning: the Athenian philosopher who let himself be overlooked

Epictetus.meaning: a Stoic teacher who grew up enslaved

mindfulness.meaning: calm, open attention to the present moment

handbook.meaning: the Enchiridion: Arrian's short book of Epictetus' teaching

notes: Enchiridion 46 paraphrased: never call yourself a philosopher; do not talk much among the uninstructed about principles but do what follows from them; at a banquet do not say how one ought to eat but eat as one ought; Socrates so avoided ostentation that people came to him wishing to be introduced to philosophers and he took them; danger of vomiting what you have not digested; when someone says you know nothing and you are not vexed, you have begun; sheep do not vomit grass but produce wool and milk.
